prompt: What crosses the connection from the server to the client when an aggregation pipeline runs?

choices.text: Every document the first stage reads
choices.why: That is what a loop in the application moves.

choices.text: Only the output of the last stage
choices.why: Right. Every earlier stage works on the server.

choices.text: The output of each stage, for the client to check
choices.why: Stages pass documents to each other on the server.

choices.text: The pipeline's source code and the matching documents
choices.why: The pipeline goes the other way, client to server.

prompt: Revenue per month in `America/Sao_Paulo` gave a `2025-12` row with 33 orders, although every order was generated in 2026. Why?

choices.text: The generator has a bug in its first day
choices.why: The dates are all in 2026 UTC; the month depends on the zone asked for.

choices.text: Decimal128 sums spill into the previous group
choices.why: The sums are exact; the row is about dates.

choices.text: $sort put a December order first by mistake
choices.why: $sort ordered thirteen groups correctly; the group key is the point.

choices.text: Early 2026 in UTC was still 2025 in São Paulo
choices.why: Right. A BSON date is a moment; the zone in $dateToString decides the calendar month.

prompt: A `$group` stage says `revenue: { $sum: "total" }`, without a dollar inside the string. What does it produce?

choices.text: A zero, silently
choices.why: Right. $sum ignores values that are not numbers, so the literal string adds nothing.

choices.text: An error naming the missing dollar
choices.why: No error: a string literal is a valid argument; it just is not a number.

choices.text: The same totals, since the field name is understood
choices.why: Without the dollar it is the text "total", not the field.

choices.text: The count of documents in each group
choices.why: Counting is $sum: 1.

prompt: What does `$unwind: "$items"` do to an order with three lines?

choices.text: Keeps the first line and drops the rest
choices.why: Every element becomes a document; none is dropped.

choices.text: Sorts the lines inside the array
choices.why: Sorting an array is a different operator.

choices.text: Makes three documents, each with one line in items
choices.why: Right. 100,000 orders became 200,652 lines.

choices.text: Merges identical lines into one
choices.why: Order 2's two identical lines came out as two documents.

prompt: Why is the `$lookup` to `products` placed after the `$group` in the best-sellers pipeline?

choices.text: $lookup cannot read documents made by $unwind
choices.why: It can; it would just run once per line.

choices.text: So it runs four times instead of about two hundred thousand
choices.why: Right. A join after the reduction works once per result.

choices.text: $group would lose the product name otherwise
choices.why: Keeping the name through a group is possible; the reason is cost.

choices.text: A lookup has to be the last stage of a pipeline
choices.why: The $project came after it.

prompt: Why does `$lookup` put its matches in an array, so that the pipeline needs `$first` to take the name out?

choices.text: Because products is a capped collection
choices.why: It is an ordinary collection.

choices.text: Because $project only reads arrays
choices.why: $project reads any field.

choices.text: To keep the products sorted by _id
choices.why: The array's purpose is the number of matches, not their order.

choices.text: To it, a SKU matches zero, one or many products
choices.why: Right. Here exactly one product matches each SKU, but the stage cannot know that.

prompt: Complete the stage that turns each element of an order's lines into its own document: `{ $___: "$items" }`.
A product page runs a `$lookup` from `orders` to `reviews` on every request to show three recent reviews. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Reconsider the model, embedding what that page reads
choices.why: Right. Lessons 3 and 4: model for the query the page makes.

choices.text: Nothing; $lookup is the normal way to read related data
choices.why: It is the exception for reports; a join on every request is a modelling smell.

choices.text: Add allowDiskUse so the join does not fail
choices.why: Three reviews never approach a memory limit.

choices.text: Move the lookup before the $match
choices.why: That makes it run on more documents, not fewer.

prompt: Over the whole collection, how many documents did `$unwind: "$items"` produce from the 100,000 orders?
The loop sent 24,564,648 bytes and the pipeline 111,198. Where do most of the pipeline's bytes come from?

choices.text: The one result document
choices.why: One small document is a few hundred bytes at most.

choices.text: The orders the $match let through
choices.why: They never left the server; only the group's output did.

choices.text: The serverStatus replies

choices.text: Index entries sent for the client to check
choices.why: No index entries are sent to a client.

prompt: The loop's revenue was `206042969.6000362` and the pipeline's `206042969.60`. What made the loop's wrong?

choices.text: It read some orders twice
choices.why: Both counted 98,958 orders.

choices.text: parseFloat turned each total into a double
choices.why: Right. The pipeline added Decimal128 values, which are exact.

choices.text: The pipeline rounded its answer to two places
choices.why: Decimal128 kept the cents exactly; nothing was rounded.

choices.text: mongosh truncates long numbers when it prints them
choices.why: It printed the double's full value; that value is off.

prompt: A nightly job must write every order of the day to a file for the accounting system. Pipeline or loop?

choices.text: A pipeline, which is faster for any job
choices.why: It is faster when the result is small; here every document is the result.

choices.text: A $group into one document holding every order
choices.why: One document is limited to 16 MB, and the data still crosses.

choices.text: Neither; the file has to be written by mongodump
choices.why: mongodump writes BSON for restoring, not a file for another system.

choices.text: A loop over a find on that day
choices.why: Right. The pipeline's advantage is sending less, and here nothing can be left behind.

prompt: How many documents did the loop fetch to compute the total?
The loop took 6,989 ms on the lab. What should you expect on your machine?

choices.text: A different time, and the same wide gap
choices.why: Right. Timings vary from run to run; the size of the gap is what holds.

choices.text: Exactly 6,989 ms, since the data is the same
choices.why: The data is the same; the machine and the moment are not.

choices.text: The pipeline being slower on a faster machine
choices.why: A faster machine speeds both up; the loop still moves 24.5 MB.

choices.text: The same time divided by your number of processors
choices.why: The loop runs in one thread of mongosh.

prompt: Which of these pipelines read the whole collection, with an index on `{ status: 1, ordered_at: -1 }`?

choices.text: $match on status, then $group by customer
choices.why: A $match first became an IXSCAN.

choices.text: $group by status, then $match on _id
choices.why: The server moved that match before the group and used the index.

choices.text: $group by customer, then $match on its list
choices.why: Right. The match depends on what the group computed, so it cannot move.

choices.text: $match on status and ordered_at, then $sort by ordered_at
choices.why: Equality then sort is what this index is for.

prompt: Since MongoDB 6.0, what happens by default when a sort stage passes its 100 MB?

choices.text: The pipeline fails with a memory error
choices.why: That happens only with allowDiskUse: false.

choices.text: It writes sorted runs to disk and merges them
choices.why: Right: usedDisk: true and a count of spills in explain.

choices.text: The server raises the limit for that query
choices.why: The limit stays; the stage spills past it.

choices.text: It keeps the first 100 MB and drops the rest
choices.why: Dropping input would give a wrong answer; nothing is dropped.

prompt: Match each explain or error result to the run that produced it, sorting 29 MB of orders.
hint: One description belongs to none of them.

pairs.right: limit at 10 MB and allowDiskUse: false
limit at 10 MB and the default

prompt: An explain shows `usedDisk: true` on a `$group`. Which changes reduce the memory it needs? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: A $match before it that sends fewer documents in
choices.why: Yes: less input, less to hold.

choices.text: A $project early on that drops fields no later stage reads
choices.why: Yes: the memory counted is what each document still carries.

choices.text: Passing allowDiskUse: false
choices.why: That turns the spill into a failure; the memory needed is the same.

choices.text: Raising the server's memory limit for everyone
choices.why: The stage needs as much as before; the server just holds more at once.

prompt: A report groups paid orders by customer and keeps the customers with ten or more. Where should the filter on `status` go, and why?

choices.text: After the $group, so every order is counted first
choices.why: Counting unpaid orders would give the wrong count, and the group reads everything.

choices.text: In the client, after the results arrive
choices.why: Filtering in the client moves every group across first.

choices.text: In a $lookup to a collection of statuses
choices.why: status is a field of the order; no join is needed.

choices.text: In a $match before the $group
choices.why: Right: there it uses an index on status. The match on 'ten or more' goes after, since it is on what the group computed.

choices.text: Send each order's confirmation e-mail again
choices.why: Every order has to reach the program to be sent.

choices.text: Copy every order to another system
choices.why: Every document crosses either way.

choices.text: Show one order's page to its customer
